section.title: The Shrewd Manager and the Rich Man and Lazarus
section.sectionRationale: Jesus tells of a manager about to be fired who shrewdly uses his master's wealth to secure his future, and He turns the story into a summons to use money now for eternal ends, for no one can serve both God and money. The money-loving Pharisees scoff, so Jesus warns them with the account of a rich man who feasted while Lazarus starved at his gate, and who woke in torment across an unbridgeable chasm. Those who will not hear Moses and the Prophets will not be persuaded even by one who rises from the dead.
section.thesis: Money is a servant to be spent for eternity or a master that damns, so Jesus calls His people to shrewd, faithful, generous stewardship in light of the world to come, and warns that a heart deaf to Scripture will not be changed even by a resurrection.
section.frameNote: Three movements: the parable of the shrewd manager and its lessons on money; the scoffing Pharisees, the law, and the kingdom; and the rich man and Lazarus, the great chasm, and the sufficiency of Moses and the Prophets.

units.label: The shrewd manager
units.note: use worldly wealth to make friends for eternity

verses.text: Jesus also said to His disciples, “There was a rich man whose manager was accused of wasting his possessions.
So he called him in to ask, ‘What is this I hear about you? Turn in an account of your management, for you cannot be manager any longer.’
The manager said to himself, ‘What shall I do, now that my master is taking away my position? I am too weak to dig and too ashamed to beg.
I know what I will do so that after my removal from management, people will welcome me into their homes.’
And he called in each one of his master’s debtors. ‘How much do you owe my master?’ he asked the first.
‘A hundred measures of olive oil,’ he answered. ‘Take your bill,’ said the manager, ‘sit down quickly, and write fifty.’
Then he asked another, ‘And how much do you owe?’ ‘A hundred measures of wheat,’ he replied. ‘Take your bill and write eighty,’ he told him.
The master commended the dishonest manager because he had acted {{phronimos|shrewdly}}. For the sons of this age are more shrewd in dealing with their own kind than are the sons of light.
I tell you, use worldly wealth to make friends for yourselves so that when it is gone, they will welcome you into eternal dwellings.

units.label: Faithful with money, and two masters
units.note: you cannot serve both God and money

verses.text: Whoever is {{pistos|faithful}} with very little will also be faithful with much, and whoever is dishonest with very little will also be dishonest with much.
So if you have not been faithful with worldly wealth, who will entrust you with true riches?
And if you have not been faithful with the belongings of another, who will give you belongings of your own?
No servant can serve two masters. Either he will hate the one and love the other, or he will be devoted to the one and despise the other. You cannot serve both God and {{mamonas|money}}.”

units.label: The scoffing Pharisees, the law, and the kingdom
units.note: what is prized among men is detestable before God

verses.text: The Pharisees, who were lovers of money, heard all of this and were scoffing at Jesus.
So He said to them, “You are the ones who justify yourselves before men, but God knows your hearts. For what is prized among men is detestable before God.
The Law and the Prophets were proclaimed until John. Since that time, the gospel of the kingdom of God is being preached, and everyone is forcing his way into it.
But it is easier for heaven and earth to pass away than for a single stroke of a pen to drop out of the Law.
Anyone who divorces his wife and marries another woman commits adultery, and he who marries a divorced woman commits adultery.

units.label: The rich man and Lazarus
units.note: they have Moses and the Prophets

verses.text: Now there was a rich man dressed in purple and fine linen, who lived each day in joyous splendor.
And a beggar named Lazarus lay at his gate, covered with sores
and longing to be fed with the crumbs that fell from the rich man’s table. Even the dogs came and licked his sores.
One day the beggar died and was carried by the angels to Abraham’s side. And the rich man also died and was buried.
In Hades, where he was in torment, he looked up and saw Abraham from afar, with Lazarus by his side.
So he cried out, ‘Father Abraham, have mercy on me and send Lazarus to dip the tip of his finger in water and cool my tongue. For I am in agony in this fire.’
But Abraham answered, ‘Child, remember that during your lifetime you received your good things, while Lazarus received bad things. But now he is comforted here, while you are in agony.
And besides all this, a great {{chasma|chasm}} has been fixed between us and you, so that even those who wish cannot cross from here to you, nor can anyone cross from there to us.’
‘Then I beg you, father,’ he said, ‘send Lazarus to my father’s house,
for I have five brothers. Let him warn them, so that they will not also end up in this place of torment.’
But Abraham replied, ‘They have Moses and the Prophets; let your brothers listen to them.’
‘No, father Abraham,’ he said, ‘but if someone is sent to them from the dead, they will repent.’
Then Abraham said to him, ‘If they do not listen to Moses and the Prophets, they will not be persuaded even if someone rises from the dead.’”

phronimos.gloss: Prudent, shrewd, sensible. The master commends the dishonest manager not for his dishonesty but for his foresight: facing a crisis, he acted decisively to secure his future. Jesus wishes the sons of light were as clear-eyed and urgent about eternity as the sons of this age are about money.

pistos.gloss: Faithful, trustworthy. How a person handles money, a very little thing, reveals whether he can be trusted with true and lasting riches. Faithfulness in small, worldly stewardship is the training ground and the test for greater things God would entrust.

mamonas.gloss: Mammon, money or wealth personified as a rival master. Jesus does not merely say wealth is dangerous; He makes it a would-be lord that competes with God for the heart's devotion. One cannot be a slave to both; money must be servant or it becomes god.

chasma.gloss: A chasm, a gaping gulf. Between the comforted Lazarus and the tormented rich man a great gulf has been fixed, uncrossable in either direction. The word underlines the finality of the divide beyond death, and the urgency of hearing God's word now, while the gate of mercy still stands open.

basic.context: Jesus tells His disciples of a manager caught wasting his master's goods and about to be fired. Before the axe falls, he shrewdly reduces what his master's debtors owe, so they will take him in later. The master commends his foresight, and Jesus draws the lesson: use money now for eternal ends, be faithful with it, and remember that you cannot serve both God and money. The Pharisees, who loved money, scoff. So Jesus tells of a rich man who feasted daily while a beggar named Lazarus starved at his gate. Both die: Lazarus is carried to Abraham's side, the rich man wakes in torment. A great chasm now divides them. The rich man begs that his brothers be warned, but Abraham says they have Moses and the Prophets; if they will not hear them, they will not believe even a resurrection.
basic.hermeneutics: Read the chapter as teaching on money in the light of eternity. The parable is not praising dishonesty but urgency and foresight. The sayings apply it: be faithful, choose your master. The Lazarus story then dramatizes the eternal stakes and warns that a heart deaf to Scripture will not be moved even by a miracle.
basic.originalLanguages: The manager acted phronimos, shrewdly, with foresight about his future. Disciples are called to be pistos, faithful, with money, a very little thing. No one can serve both God and mamonas, money treated as a rival master. And beyond death a great chasma, an uncrossable gulf, is fixed between comfort and torment.
basic.typology: The rich man's ignored gate recalls the covenant call to care for the poor at your doors. Abraham's side pictures the gathering of the faithful to their father in the age to come. And the closing line about one rising from the dead points ahead to Jesus' own resurrection, which a hardened generation would still refuse.
basic.christ: Jesus is the true and faithful Steward who spends everything, even His life, for others, and the poor man's advocate against the callous rich. He is the One who will rise from the dead, the sign the rich man's brothers would not need if they heard Moses and the Prophets, and the One to whom all the Scriptures point.
basic.god: God knows the heart behind the money-loving self-justification of men, and He counts as detestable what people prize. He receives the ignored beggar and comforts him, and He upholds a settled justice beyond death. He speaks sufficiently in His written word, so that those who will not hear it have no excuse.
basic.crossReferences: Matthew 6 gives the same saying, you cannot serve God and money. 1 Timothy 6 warns that the love of money is a root of all kinds of evil. Deuteronomy 15 commands open-handed care for the poor at your gate. John 11 shows a different Lazarus raised, yet many still would not believe.
basic.oneStory: As He nears Jerusalem, Jesus presses His people to hold money loosely and spend it for eternity, warning that it can become a master that damns. The rich man and Lazarus reveal the eternal weight of how we live now, and the closing word, they have Moses and the Prophets, points to the sufficiency of Scripture and to the risen Christ whom it all foretells.

context.literary:
Luke 16 is one long address with two halves, and the seam between them is verse 14. The first half, 16:1-13, is spoken to the disciples and holds a parable about a manager with a string of sayings attached to it. The second, 16:14-31, is spoken in the hearing of Pharisees who are 'lovers of money' and who sneer, and it holds a short block of sayings and a second parable. The two parables are mirrors. In the first a rich man's agent deals with money in a way that earns him friends; in the second a rich man himself deals with a poor man in a way that earns him none. The first ends in an invitation to be welcomed into 'eternal dwellings,' 16:9, the second in a rich man who cannot be welcomed anywhere, 16:26.

The chapter follows the three parables of chapter 15 and carries their themes forward. The younger son in 15:13 'squandered' his property, and Luke uses the same verb for the manager in 16:1 who is accused of squandering his master's. The father's feast in chapter 15 is described with a verb for merrymaking, and the same verb returns for the rich man in 16:19, who 'lived each day in joyous splendor.' It is also the verb of the rich fool's self-address in 12:19. A single word links a prodigal, a fool and a rich man at his gate.

The sayings in 16:10-13 are knit by a repeated word. 'Faithful' and 'dishonest' recur in verses 10 to 12, and the chain of 'very little,' 'much,' 'worldly wealth,' 'true riches,' 'another's' and 'your own' builds an argument from small to great. Verse 13 then sums up the first half in a single choice of masters.

The middle section, 16:14-18, is difficult to place and is often called a puzzle. It joins the reaction of the Pharisees, a statement about the law and the prophets, a word about the kingdom, and a saying on divorce. The thread is the law: the Pharisees honor it outwardly while loving money, and Jesus says that it has not lost a stroke. The rich man story then shows the law's own voice, Moses and the Prophets, as the one witness that should have governed the rich man's gate.
context.historical:
The world behind the first parable is one of absentee landowners and managers. A rich man might hold estates at a distance and entrust their running to an agent, who could negotiate leases, collect rents in produce and sign contracts in his master's name. That is why the debtors in 16:5-7 respond when the manager speaks. The sums are very large. The BSB footnote at 16:6 explains that a hundred baths of oil is about 870 gallons, and the footnote at 16:7 says that a hundred cors of wheat is probably about thirty tons. These were commercial tenants, not poor peasants, and the reductions of fifty and twenty measures were gifts of real size.

How the manager's reductions are to be understood is a matter of debate. Some think the manager cut his own commission, which an agent could take as part of the bill. Others point out that the law forbade interest on loans to fellow Israelites, Exodus 22:25 and Deuteronomy 23:19, so that debts in kind often hid an interest charge, and that the manager may have struck it out. Whatever the arithmetic, the setting explains why the master could shrug and commend his clever planning: the debtors were now grateful to him and bound to the manager as friends.

In the second story, purple cloth and fine linen marked the wealthiest class. Purple dye was costly, and linen was the best undergarment. The beggar lay at the rich man's gate, a gateway to a courtyard or house of consequence, and he longed for what fell from the table. Dogs in that world were scavengers rather than pets, and they offered the sores of Lazarus no comfort. To be 'carried by the angels' to Abraham's side, 16:22, evoked a feast, since the Greek is literally Abraham's bosom, the place of a favored reclining guest at a banquet, a position John 13:23 describes for the disciple beside Jesus. In Jewish thought of the time, the dead awaited resurrection in a place of rest or distress, and Hades was the name for the realm of the dead.

The Pharisees, according to Luke, loved money, 16:14, and Luke has already pronounced woe on the rich, 6:24, and charged the Pharisees with greed, 11:39. The divorce saying in 16:18 touches the dispute over Deuteronomy 24:1-4, and it may also remind Luke's readers of John the Baptist's rebuke of Herod Antipas over his marriage, Luke 3:19-20.
context.canonical:
The Old Testament speaks with one voice about wealth and the poor, and the rich man in the second story is judged by it. The law commands open-handedness toward the poor brother at the gate, Deuteronomy 15:7-11, and Proverbs says that whoever is kind to the poor lends to the LORD, Proverbs 19:17. The prophets pronounce woe on those who lie on beds of ivory and feast on lambs while the nation falls apart, Amos 6:4-7, and the first to go into exile are those who reclined at ease, which is the destiny of the rich man. Isaiah 58:7 calls for sharing bread with the hungry. Psalm 49 teaches that no one can ransom his own life, and that the rich who trust in their wealth die like the beasts. Job 31:16-23 shows a righteous man who refused to eat his food alone.

Jesus' teaching on the two masters is known from Matthew 6:24. Luke has already told of the rich fool, 12:13-21, and of the call to sell possessions and give alms, 12:33-34, and Paul will carry the theme into the church: the love of money is a root of all kinds of evil, 1 Timothy 6:10, and the rich are to be generous so that they take hold of life that is truly life, 6:17-19. Luke's picture of early believers holding all things in common, Acts 4:32-37, is the church doing 16:9.

The sufficiency of Moses and the Prophets recurs in Luke. On the road to Emmaus the risen Jesus begins with Moses and all the Prophets and interprets to the two travelers the things about Himself, Luke 24:25-27, and in 24:44-47 He says that everything written about Him in the Law, the Prophets and the Psalms had to be fulfilled. John 5:46-47 says that Moses wrote about Jesus. The last line of the parable, that one who rises from the dead will not persuade, finds a grim echo in John 11:43-53 and 12:9-11, where the raising of another Lazarus leads the chief priests to plot to kill both Jesus and Lazarus, and in the Easter story itself, where the report of the resurrection is bought off with silver, Matthew 28:11-15.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Luke wants disciples and Pharisees alike to see that money is a spiritual matter before it is an economic one. For the disciples, the lesson of the manager is that the present is a time of reckoning and opportunity. A man who has lost his position does not wring his hands; he acts while he still has the books. The 'sons of light' are meant to bring that clarity to the end of the age, and to spend what is not really theirs on what will last, so that they are welcomed when it is gone.

For the Pharisees, the message is sharper. They have heard Jesus on the choice of masters and they scoff, and Jesus answers by naming what they do: they justify themselves before people while God reads the heart. The story of the rich man and Lazarus is not told to give a map of the afterlife. It is told to make them see that the man in torment is the man whom they could become, and that the beggar at his gate was the person the law had been pointing to all along.

Luke also means us to take the last lines seriously. The rich man begs for a sign for his brothers, and Abraham refuses, because the problem is not lack of evidence. People who will not listen to Scripture will not be moved by a miracle. Luke is writing after Easter, and he knows that his readers have heard about a resurrection. The question the chapter leaves with them is whether they are listening to Moses and the Prophets, and what the listening has done to their hands.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The two parables are narrated pictures, and their details should not be treated as a program. Jesus does not tell his followers to defraud an employer; the master calls the manager dishonest even while praising his foresight. And the story of the rich man and Lazarus does not give a full account of what happens at death, with a conversation across a gap. Its purpose is to say what matters, and the details serve that.

The sayings in 16:9-13 are prescriptive and clear. Use worldly wealth to make friends for eternity. Be faithful in what is small. Do not try to serve God and money. The first of these commands is aimed at the use of resources, not the pursuit of them: the manager's gift is that he spends what he has been given and does not hoard it. The second tells us that stewardship of money is a test of readiness for greater trust.

The story of the rich man is descriptive of a judgment, and it prescribes by implication that those who have means should see the Lazarus at the gate. It does not say that wealth itself is the sin or that poverty is itself the virtue; Abraham himself was rich. The sin is a life lived on a table where the beggar is never seen. Nor does the story tell us that the dead can speak to the living. It is not a template for contacting them, and its warning about listening to Scripture is the lasting part.

The saying on divorce, 16:18, is a command and is placed in a context about the abiding authority of the law. It should be read with the other Gospel treatments of the subject, Matthew 5:31-32, Matthew 19:3-9 and Mark 10:2-12, and its application should be pastoral as well as exact.

debates.question: What exactly is commended in the shrewd manager?

views.label: His decisive foresight, not his dishonesty
views.case: The text calls him the dishonest manager even as it commends his shrewdness; what is praised is that, facing a reckoning, he acted urgently and cleverly to secure his future. Jesus laments that the sons of light lack this same clear-eyed urgency about eternity, and applies it to using money for lasting good.

views.label: A lightening of unjust debts or the steward's own commission
views.case: Some argue he was cancelling the interest or his own cut rather than defrauding the master, which would explain the master's approval on honest grounds. On this reading the manager repents of exploitation and acts justly, and is praised for genuine good, not mere cleverness.

debates.bearing: Either way the application is the same: money is fleeting and the reckoning is sure, so use worldly wealth now, decisively and generously, for friends and treasure that outlast it.

debates.question: How should the rich man and Lazarus be read?

views.label: A parable teaching the eternal stakes of how we live and hear
views.case: Like the surrounding parables it uses vivid, culturally familiar imagery to make a moral and spiritual point: wealth wrongly held damns, the ignored poor are precious to God, and Scripture is sufficient to warn. The details serve the message rather than mapping the afterlife precisely.

views.label: A window onto the reality of conscious existence after death
views.case: Whatever its parabolic form, Jesus affirms real states beyond death, comfort and torment, memory and longing, and a fixed, uncrossable divide. The story presses the sober truth that eternity is settled by this life and cannot be renegotiated later.

debates.bearing: Both hold together the urgency Jesus intends: this life matters eternally, the poor at our gate matter to God, and the time to hear His word and repent is now, before the chasm is fixed.

debates.question: What does 'everyone is forcing his way into it' mean in verse 16?

views.label: An eager, even desperate, pressing into the kingdom
views.case: The verb can be taken as a middle, 'everyone is pressing eagerly into it,' or as a passive, which is the BSB footnote's 'Or everyone is urged to enter into it.' Either fits the picture of tax collectors and sinners crowding toward Jesus in 15:1. The gospel is being preached, and those who hear it are pushing in, in contrast to the Pharisees who stay outside.

views.label: Violent opposition or false seizing of the kingdom
views.case: Others hear the verb as a passive or as a hostile one, as many take the related saying in Matthew 11:12, so that the kingdom is being attacked or grasped by force. In that case the words describe the pressure of those who try to take the kingdom by their own means, as the Pharisees with their self-justification.

debates.bearing: The passage is hard, and the grammar leaves room for both readings. What is not in doubt is the contrast with the law's era: since John, the kingdom is being preached, and it demands a response of the whole person, not a quiet assent.

study.originalLanguages:
The manager in 16:1 is an oikonomos, a household steward, from which the word 'economy' descends. Luke has used the same word in 12:42, where Jesus asks who is the 'faithful and wise manager' whom the master will set over his household. Faithful and wise, pistos and phronimos, are the very two words that chapter 16 puts side by side in a manager who is wise but not faithful. The parable reads as a reply to the earlier question: here is a steward who understands the moment but has not been trustworthy, and the sayings that follow call disciples to be both.

The charge against him in 16:1 is that he was 'accused,' a rendering of diaballo, which means to bring charges and is the verb from which diabolos, 'devil' or 'slanderer,' is formed. The master's decision is blunt: turn in the account, since you can no longer be manager. When he is commended in 16:8, he is called 'the manager of unrighteousness,' literally, and the next verse speaks of the 'mammon of unrighteousness,' which the BSB renders 'worldly wealth.' The adjective is adikos, and it comes back in 16:10 as the opposite of faithful. Jesus does not pretend the money is clean. He tells the disciples to use something that is touched by the world's unrighteousness for ends that last.

The result is 'eternal dwellings,' 16:9, and the Greek noun is skenai, tents or tabernacles. A lifetime of earthly houses ends, and the friends one has made by giving are those who will receive one into a dwelling that does not fold up. The word recalls the tents of the exodus and the tabernacle, and it adds to Luke's theme of being welcomed.

'Master' in 16:8 is kyrios, and the sentence has sometimes been read as Jesus' own comment, since Luke often uses kyrios of Jesus in narration, as in 18:6. The context of the parable favors the wealthy man, because the debtors were his, but the doubled use of the word in 16:8 and 16:13 is part of the chapter's play on who the true Lord is.

The household servant in 16:13 is oiketes, a slave who lives in a particular house, and the verb for serving, douleuo, is the one for a slave's work. Luke's wording is more domestic than Matthew's parallel and closes the options: a slave belongs to one house. The two attitudes are paired verbs, hate and love, and then 'be devoted to' and 'despise.' The first of the second pair, antechomai, means to hold firmly to something, to cling. The second, kataphroneo, means to think down on. The choice is between what one holds to and what one looks down on.

In 16:14 the Pharisees are philarguroi, 'lovers of money,' a compound that returns in 2 Timothy 3:2. They 'scoffed,' and the verb ekmukterizo literally means to turn up the nose at someone. Luke uses it again in 23:35 when the rulers sneer at Jesus on the cross. In 16:15 what is 'prized' among people is hypselon, the high or lofty thing, and it is a bdelugma before God, a detestable thing, the word the Septuagint uses for idols and abominations. The same pride that Jesus described at the table of chapter 14 is here named as an abomination.

Finally, the stroke of the pen in 16:17 is the keraia, literally a little horn, the smallest mark of a letter. The 'chasm' of 16:26 'has been fixed,' and the verb is a perfect from sterizo, a settled state. Luke used the same root for Jesus in 9:51, where He 'set His face' toward Jerusalem. The fixedness of the gulf and the resolve of Jesus are two uses of one verb, a reminder that God's purposes, once set, stand.

typology.type: The manager and the faithful steward
typology.fulfillment: The picture of a servant entrusted with a master's goods runs through Scripture, from Joseph in Potiphar's house, Genesis 39:4-6, to the household managers of Luke 12:42-48. The correspondence in Christ is that He is the one steward who spent everything of His Father's on those who owed a debt they could not pay. The cancellation of debts in the parable looks forward to the forgiveness of debts in the Lord's Prayer, Luke 11:4, and to the cross, where the record of debt that stood against us was set aside, Colossians 2:14. The type breaks down at the point of honesty: the manager was dishonest, while Christ was faithful in all.

The poor man laid at the gate is a figure of the poor of the law and the prophets, the neighbor whose need is a test of the whole community. In Christ, the Lord Himself comes to the gate. Jesus identifies with the hungry and sick, Matthew 25:35-40, and 'though He was rich, yet for your sake He became poor,' as 2 Corinthians 8:9 says. The type falls short because Lazarus is simply a victim, while the Christ who stands at the door brings the feast, and the one who takes the lowly place is the one who is exalted, Philippians 2:7-9.

typology.type: Abraham's side, the place of the blessed
typology.fulfillment: Abraham was the one to whom God promised blessing for all nations, and in Jewish thought of the time his side was where the righteous were gathered. Jesus uses it as a picture of comfort. In Christ the destination of the faithful is stated more fully: to depart and be with Christ, Philippians 1:23, and to be with Him in Paradise, as He promises the thief in Luke 23:43. Hebrews 11:16 speaks of a better country. The type falls short in that Abraham is a host who can receive but cannot rescue, whereas Christ is the one who opens the way.

typology.type: The one who rises from the dead
typology.fulfillment: The refusal of Abraham to send someone from the dead points ahead to Easter. When Jesus is raised, those who held to Moses and the Prophets, like the Emmaus pair, find that the Scriptures speak of Him, Luke 24:25-27, and those who will not hear are not persuaded, Matthew 28:11-15. It escalates in Paul's insistence that Christ is raised according to the Scriptures, 1 Corinthians 15:3-4. The type falls short in one respect: the Lazarus of the parable is never sent, while Christ is sent, and rises, and the verdict of the parable is borne out.

study.christ:
Luke 16 leads to Christ first as the Lord who knows and judges the heart. The Pharisees justified themselves before people, 16:15, but He sees the heart, and that sight is the same by which He reads the whole chapter. He is the true Master in a chapter about masters, and the question of 16:13 is finally a question about Him. When Jesus says that no one can serve two masters, He is not only stating a principle, He is claiming the allegiance that money wants.

He is also the pattern for what the chapter commands. The disciples are told to use what is not their own to make friends who will welcome them, and no one has spent more freely than the One who, though rich, became poor so that we might become rich, 2 Corinthians 8:9. The manager cut the debts of others in a clever scheme and was commended; Christ cancels the record of debt that stood against us, nailing it to the cross, Colossians 2:14. The comparison is not exact and should not be pressed, since the manager's story is a parable about prudence and not a picture of atonement. But the call to settle accounts in the light of eternity finds its fullest answer in the One who paid what He did not owe.

He is the advocate of the Lazarus at the gate. In Luke 4:18 He announces good news for the poor, and in 6:20 He says they are blessed, and the beggar who is named and comforted in the second story is the kind of person to whom He comes. The rich man is not condemned for being rich but for never seeing the man at his gate, and Jesus is the one who sees. He lays down His life for the very people the rich man walks past.

And He is the one who rises. The last line of the chapter, that even one who rises from the dead will not be heard by those who refuse Scripture, is a quiet prophecy. After the resurrection, the risen Christ opens the Scriptures, beginning with Moses and all the Prophets, Luke 24:27, and says that everything written about Him must be fulfilled, 24:44. The Scriptures are not set against the resurrection. They are the way to see Him.

A caution belongs here. The chapter does not turn the manager into a picture of Jesus, and the rich man is not an allegory of any single group. The links above rest on Luke's own pattern, in which Jesus is the Lord who calls to account, the friend of the poor, and the one to whom Moses and the Prophets point. What this chapter adds is the sober warning that the same Christ who gives an invitation also speaks of a chasm.
study.god:
The God of Luke 16 is a God who sees. The Pharisees justify themselves before people, but 'God knows your hearts,' 16:15, and the whole chapter is a lesson in what that knowledge means. He sees a manager's scheming and a rich man's blind eye. He sees a beggar who is covered in sores and lying at a gate that no one opens. What the world prizes, God calls an abomination, and so the values of those who love money are not just mistaken; they are opposed to God.

He is the God who owns everything and entrusts it to people. The language of the manager and of 16:12, belongings 'of another,' makes it plain that what we hold is held on loan. That is the root of faithfulness: we are not owners but stewards, and the day of accounting is coming. The very word for a manager gives theology a household shape, with one Master over all.

He is a God who exalts the lowly and cares for the poor. The only person in all of Jesus' parables who is given a name is a beggar. The name Lazarus is a form of Eleazar, 'God helps,' and the story says that God did exactly that. Angels carry him. The rich man is never named in the story, and the contrast of the named and the nameless says something about what God remembers.

He is a God of settled justice. The chasm of 16:26 'has been fixed,' and the language of reckoning in the whole chapter says that the lives of people matter forever. At the same time, He is the God who pleads in His word: the sufficiency of Moses and the Prophets means that He has not left anyone without a witness. If the rich man's brothers perish, it will not be because God was silent.

This keeps two truths together that the world often splits. God is generous: the parable of the manager is about grace received and shared, and the call is to be welcomed into 'eternal dwellings.' And God is exacting: He is the one who will hold stewards to account, and who will not be bought by a sign. The call to worship is to give Him what the manager gave his master's debtors: a quick, wholehearted response while there is still time. A people who listen to His word, who see the people at their gate, and who hold their money loosely because they love their Master are the people this chapter is written to make.

crossReferences.note: Jesus asks who is the faithful and wise manager whom the master will set over his household, and warns the manager who abuses his trust. The shrewd manager of Luke 16 is a negative example of the same figure, and the two passages together define what faithful stewardship is.

The rich fool tells himself to relax, eat, drink and be merry, and God calls him a fool and says his life is required of him. He is the first of Luke's rich men whose present comfort hides the coming reckoning, and the rich man at the gate in Luke 16 is his successor.

The younger son squandered his property in wild living. Luke uses the same verb of the manager in 16:1, and the link makes the first parable of chapter 16 a second look at squandering, this time by a steward with someone else's wealth.
Whoever is kind to the poor lends to the LORD, and He will repay. It supplies the logic of Luke 16:9 and 16:25: what is given to the poor is not lost, and what is withheld is not forgotten.

Those who lie on beds of ivory and eat the choicest lambs, who are not grieved over the ruin of Joseph, will be the first to go into exile, and the revelry of the loungers will end. The picture closely matches the rich man's life of splendor and his sudden end.

When there is a poor man among your brothers in any town, you must not harden your heart or shut your hand, but open it. The law's own demand lies behind Abraham's words that the rich man's brothers have Moses and the Prophets, and it shows that the gate of Lazarus was a failure to obey Moses.

The love of money is a root of all kinds of evil, and some who craved it have wandered from the faith. Paul applies the choice between God and money to the church, and it shows the Pharisees' trouble in Luke 16:14 was not unique to them.

The rich are told not to trust in uncertain riches but to do good and be generous, so that they store up a good foundation for the coming age. It is nearly a commentary on Luke 16:9, with the same idea of using present wealth for future welcome.

On the road to Emmaus the risen Jesus begins with Moses and all the Prophets and explains what the Scriptures say about Himself. It shows that the sufficiency of Moses and the Prophets in Luke 16:29-31 is not a closed door but the way to recognize the risen Lord.

Jesus calls a man named Lazarus out of the tomb, and some believe, but others report it to the Pharisees, who gather the council. It is a sharp echo of Luke 16:31, which says that people who do not listen to Scripture will not be persuaded by someone who rises from the dead.

Christ was rich and yet for the sake of believers became poor, so that they might become rich through His poverty. The use of wealth for others which Luke 16 asks of the disciple is first the pattern of Christ Himself.

study.oneStory:
The Bible begins with a world entrusted to human care. In Genesis 1:28 the man and woman are given rule over the earth, and in Genesis 2:15 they are set in the garden to work it and keep it. That is the first stewardship. The fall is the story of a steward who decides that what he holds is his own, and ever after people have clung to what they were meant to manage. Greed, the love of money and the neglect of the poor are the long consequence.

The story of Israel gives the stewardship a form. The land is the LORD's, Leviticus 25:23, and the poor are to be cared for, since they are the neighbors at the gate, Deuteronomy 15. The prophets complain again and again that the wealthy have forgotten both. When Jesus tells the story of the rich man and Lazarus, He is speaking in the voice of Moses and the Prophets, and He is saying that the covenant has not changed.

In Luke's Gospel, the chapter stands in the shadow of the coming cross. Jesus is on the road to Jerusalem, and He warns that a day of reckoning is near. The shrewd manager is the clear-eyed disciple who acts before the books are called in. The rich man is the person who thinks the books will never be called in. And the Pharisees who sneer are the people who stand between, loving money and calling it righteousness. The question the chapter presses is the question of every age: whom do you serve?

The story moves toward resolution in the one who gave up His riches. In Christ the steward of God's world has come, and He has spent Himself on others. He rises from the dead, and as Luke 24 shows, He sends His people back to Moses and the Prophets to see that the story was about Him all along. The early church practices the lesson: it holds possessions loosely, Acts 4:32-35, and gives to those in need.

At the end, the fixed chasm is gone for those who belong to Christ. In the new creation, there is no more death or mourning or crying or pain, Revelation 21:4. The poor are not forgotten and the rich who have used their wealth for God are welcomed into 'eternal dwellings.' The stewards of the world give an account, and the Master of the house invites the faithful servant into his own joy, Matthew 25:21. The world that was entrusted to humans is returned to the care of a people who finally handle it with open hands.

quiz.q: Why does the master commend the shrewd manager?

options.text: For his decisive foresight in preparing for his future, not for his dishonesty.
options.note: Luke 16:8 praises his shrewdness while still calling him the dishonest manager.

options.text: Because he acted cleverly to secure a welcome for himself.
options.note: True to the story, but it omits that the commendation is for foresight, and the man remains 'dishonest'.

options.text: Because cheating the master turned out to be acceptable.
options.note: The dishonesty is not endorsed; only the urgent foresight is held up as an example.

options.text: Because he faithfully repaid everything he had wasted.
options.note: He did not repay; he reduced the debtors' bills to win their favor.

quiz.q: What does Jesus teach about God and money?

options.text: No one can serve two masters; you cannot serve both God and money.
options.note: Luke 16:13 makes money a rival master to God, not merely a danger.

options.text: Money is dangerous and should be handled with care.
options.note: True but weaker; Jesus says money is a competing master, not just a risk.

options.text: Wealth is always sinful and must be given away entirely.
options.note: Jesus calls for faithful stewardship and generosity, not a blanket condemnation of possessions.

options.text: You can serve God and money if you keep them balanced.
options.note: Jesus explicitly denies this; you cannot serve both.

quiz.q: What was the rich man's failure in the story of Lazarus?

options.text: He feasted in splendor while ignoring the starving Lazarus at his own gate.
options.note: Luke 16:19-21 sets his daily luxury against the beggar he stepped past.

options.text: He was rich and lived comfortably.
options.note: Wealth itself is not the charge; his callous neglect of the poor at his gate is.

options.text: He failed to give Lazarus a proper burial.
options.note: The issue is his neglect in life, not funeral arrangements.

options.text: He gave away too much and impoverished himself.
options.note: The opposite: he hoarded his splendor and ignored the needy.

quiz.q: What does the great chasm signify?

options.text: A fixed, uncrossable divide beyond death, showing eternity is settled by this life.
options.note: Luke 16:26 describes a gulf no one can cross, underlining the finality of the divide.

options.text: That the rich man and Lazarus were now far apart.
options.note: True but shallow; the point is that the separation is permanent and cannot be crossed.

options.text: A temporary barrier that mercy might later remove.
options.note: The chasm is fixed and uncrossable; it is not portrayed as temporary.

options.text: That the afterlife has no real consequences.
options.note: The chasm precisely establishes real and lasting consequences.

quiz.q: What is Abraham's final answer to the rich man's plea for his brothers?

options.text: They have Moses and the Prophets; if they will not hear them, they will not be persuaded even by a resurrection.
options.note: Luke 16:29-31 grounds faith in hearing Scripture, not in signs.

options.text: Scripture is enough to warn the brothers to repent.
options.note: True, but it omits the sharp point that even a resurrection will not persuade the deaf heart.

options.text: A miracle from the dead would surely make them believe.
options.note: Abraham says the opposite; the resistant will not believe even then.

options.text: Nothing could ever warn the brothers in time.
options.note: They can be warned; they have Moses and the Prophets to hear now.

questions: The manager saw his reckoning coming and acted at once. Are you as clear-eyed and urgent about eternity as you are about your finances and future security?
Jesus says you cannot serve both God and money. Be honest: which one is actually steering your decisions, your calendar, and your worries?
The rich man never noticed Lazarus at his gate. Who is the person God has placed at the edge of your comfortable life, and are you stepping over them?
How you handle a very little thing, money, reveals whether you can be trusted with true riches. What would faithful, generous stewardship look like for you this month?
Abraham said they have Moses and the Prophets. Do you truly believe Scripture is enough to change a heart, or are you waiting for a more spectacular sign before you obey what you already know?

translationNotes.note: The debts are given in Greek measures, baths of oil and cors of wheat, amounting to roughly hundreds of gallons of oil and tens of tons of wheat, enormous sums that show how much the manager was reducing to win the debtors' goodwill.

'Abraham's side' translates a Greek phrase, into Abraham's bosom, a Jewish image for the place of comfort among the blessed dead. 'Hades' is the realm of the dead; here it is a place of conscious torment for the rich man.

The clause rendered 'everyone is forcing his way into it' can also be translated 'everyone is urged to enter it'; either way it describes the pressing summons of the kingdom now proclaimed since John.
